title: Russian drones enter Polish airspace overnight; Poland and NATO allies shoot some down
place: Eastern and central Poland, including the Lublin region

impact: Part of Poland's airspace was closed for several hours and Warsaw's Chopin Airport suspended flights. evidence: Polish authorities recorded the violations and recovered drones at multiple sites, and a NATO spokesman said NATO planes engaged potential threats in allied airspace. Russia's Defense Ministry said it did not target Poland, and Belarus said it tracked drones that lost their course after jamming, while several European leaders said it appeared intentional. attribution: Polish authorities and NATO officials treated the drones as Russian, and the Arms Control Association reports that debris analysis by multiple media outlets and Polish authorities indicates Russian origin, likely Gerbera-type drones. Russia denied targeting Poland, so responsibility for sending the drones into Polish airspace, and intent, remain disputed; recorded here as suspected.

title: Drone strikes hit Port Sudan over several days, damaging fuel depots, the airport and the main power substation
summary: From 4 May 2025 drones struck military and civilian sites in Port Sudan, the army-aligned government's wartime base on the Red Sea, over several days. Reported targets include a military base near the airport, fuel depots, the airport, a hotel near the presidential residence and the city's main power substation. Military sources blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which did not claim the attacks.
impact: Fuel depots burned, air traffic was halted on 6 May at the only airport still handling international civilian flights, and a strike on the main power substation caused a blackout across the city. The maritime security firm Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. No immediate reports of casualties were given in the AFP report. Nearly all humanitarian aid into Sudan arrives through Port Sudan, and the UN chief called the reports of attacks a worrying development.
evidence: Officials of the national electricity company and the airport confirmed drone hits, AFP and Reuters correspondents or witnesses reported explosions and smoke, and Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. Blame for the strikes rests on military sources and residents, not on a claim of responsibility or an independent investigation.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where, the type of drones, and the full extent of damage and casualties. The RSF's statement did not address the attacks. Sudan's army-aligned government accused the UAE of supplying the drones to the RSF; the UAE has consistently denied backing the RSF.
attribution: Sudanese military sources blamed the RSF, and residents told Al Jazeera they believed RSF drone strikes were responsible. title: Drone strike damages the Chornobyl New Safe Confinement; IAEA later finds it lost its confinement function
place: Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, Kyiv region
summary: At about 01:50 on 14 February 2025 a drone struck the New Safe Confinement, the structure covering the destroyed Unit 4 reactor at the Chornobyl site, and caused a fire. The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion and saw a breach of the outer layer. In late 2025 the IAEA reported that the strike caused significant structural damage and that the structure had lost its primary safety functions, including confinement, without permanent damage to its load-bearing structures.
impact: No casualties were reported and radiation levels inside and outside the building stayed normal and stable. The IAEA later said the strike did not lead to any release of radioactive material but caused significant structural damage affecting the confinement function and projected lifetime of the structure. Limited temporary repairs were carried out on the roof, and further temporary repairs were planned for 2026 with support from the EBRD.
evidence: The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion, saw smoke, fire and the breach, and was informed by Ukraine that a drone had struck the structure. The IAEA's later statements describe the event as a drone strike, and its comprehensive safety assessment confirmed the loss of confinement capability. The IAEA did not attribute the strike.
unknown: Who launched the drone: AP reported that it was not possible to independently confirm who was behind the strike. The IAEA statements in the cited sources do not state the drone type.
attribution: Ukraine's president said a Russian drone with a high-explosive warhead hit the shell. A Kremlin spokesman denied the claim, saying Russia's military does not strike nuclear facilities. The IAEA did not attribute blame.

title: Drone strikes on Tinzaouaten in northern Mali: rebel coalition says 21 civilians killed, army confirms airstrikes
summary: On 25 August 2024, airstrikes hit the village of Tinzaouatine (Tinzaouaten) in northern Mali near the Algerian border. A coalition of Tuareg-majority groups fighting for independence said drones hit a pharmacy and then people gathering nearby, killing at least 21 civilians including 11 children. Mali's General Staff confirmed airstrikes in the sector and said the precision strikes targeted terrorists.
impact: The rebel coalition's provisional toll was 21 civilians killed, including 11 children and the pharmacy manager, with dozens wounded and enormous material damage. The Associated Press described it as the largest number of civilians killed by drones since the peace agreement between the junta and pro-independence groups broke down in 2023.
evidence: The toll and the description of the targets come from the rebel coalition, a party to the conflict; the army's statement confirms airstrikes but does not address civilian casualties. Neither account is independently verified in the cited reports, and the army statement refers to airstrikes rather than drones.
unknown: The number and identity of the victims, the type of aircraft or drones used, and whether the targets were military. The army describes them as terrorists, while the rebels say civilians were killed.
attribution: Mali's General Staff confirmed airstrikes in the Tinzaouatine sector on the morning of 25 August and said they targeted terrorists. The cited reports do not name who operated the aircraft beyond the army's confirmation, and the rebel coalition's casualty claims remain unverified.

title: Houthi-claimed drone strikes central Tel Aviv, killing one person; Israeli military cites human error
place: Tel Aviv (neighbourhood near the US Embassy)
summary: At around 3:10 a.m. on 19 July 2024 an explosive drone struck central Tel Aviv, killing one person and wounding others in a neighbourhood near the US Embassy. The Houthis in Yemen claimed responsibility. Israel's military said it believed the drone was an upgraded Iranian Samad-3 that had flown from Yemen, and an Israeli military official said it was identified but penetrated Israel because of human error in operating the system.
impact: Israel's emergency services said the body of a 50-year-old man was found in an apartment close to the explosion and four people were taken to hospital with slight shrapnel injuries; AP reported at least 10 wounded, citing local police. The blast blew out windows and damaged cars over a wide area. It was described as the first lethal Houthi attack in Israel.
evidence: Israeli police and emergency services reported the casualties, and the Israeli military described the drone type and its approach from Yemen. The drone type rests on an Israeli military assessment; Israeli media reported that fragments of a drone of a kind widely used by Iranian-backed groups were recovered, and the military had not determined whether it exploded in the air or struck a building.
unknown: Whether the drone exploded in the air or hit a building, the exact number of injured (four slightly wounded in Reuters, at least 10 in AP), and the cause of the failure to sound alarms, which the military is investigating. The Houthis' claim of a new drone capable of bypassing defences was rebuffed by the Israeli military.
attribution: The Houthi spokesperson claimed responsibility on X and said the strike used a new drone called Yafa. Israel's military said it believed the drone arrived from Yemen. Analysts and Western intelligence services have long accused Iran of arming the Houthis, which Tehran denies.

title: Drone attacks hit Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant, including a reactor building, IAEA says
place: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Enerhodar area
summary: On 7 April 2024 drones struck the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the first direct targeting of the plant since November 2022 according to the IAEA. The IAEA's director general reported at least three direct hits against the main reactor containment structures, and on 9 April another drone detonated on the roof of the plant's training centre outside the site perimeter. Russia and Ukraine blamed each other.
impact: The IAEA said damage at unit 6 did not compromise nuclear safety but was a serious incident with potential to undermine the integrity of the reactor's containment system, and one casualty was reported. Russia's state nuclear agency said three people were wounded. The plant's six reactors had been shut down for months.
evidence: IAEA experts at the plant verified the impact of several drone attacks on 7 April, and on 9 April they heard a loud explosion at the time the plant said a drone detonated on the training centre roof. The IAEA team was denied access to several locations for security reasons. The director general later told the IAEA Board the strike did not compromise nuclear safety in a serious way.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where: the IAEA did not attribute the attacks. The drone type is not stated in the cited sources. The IAEA could not visit several of the locations where the plant reported attacks.
attribution: Plant officials said Ukrainian military drones carried out the attack, and Russia's IAEA ambassador accused the agency of being afraid to say Ukraine was behind it. Ukraine's UN ambassador called the strike a false flag operation by Russia. The IAEA director general said that whoever is behind the attacks is playing with fire and did not attribute them.

title: Anti-junta forces say 29 drones targeted Naypyidaw military sites; junta says it shot down seven
place: Naypyidaw (military headquarters, Aye Lar air base and Naypyidaw International Airport)
summary: On the morning of 4 April 2024 anti-junta forces attacked the Myanmar capital Naypyidaw with drones in a rare strike on the military regime's stronghold. The shadow National Unity Government said 29 explosive-laden drones targeted the military headquarters and an air base. The junta said its air defences shot down seven drones near the airport and a township and that there was no damage or casualties.
impact: Accounts conflict. The National Unity Government said preliminary reports indicated there were casualties, while the junta said there was no damage or casualties. A source at the airport said it was temporarily closed and a drone carrying a bomb was defused, and a civilian witness quoted by Myanmar Now said the drones landed at the edge of the airport runway.
evidence: The attack is described by both sides: the junta displayed images of downed drones and said it had seized 13, and anti-junta groups published photos of the drones used. Casualty and damage claims come from the parties and are not independently verified; residents near the targeted sites told RFA they were unaware of the attacks.
unknown: How many drones were launched, whether any reached their targets, and whether anyone was hurt. The numbers claimed by the sides (29 launched; seven shot down; 13 seized) cannot be reconciled from the cited sources.
attribution: The shadow National Unity Government and the anti-junta Shar Htoo Waw's Kloud Drone Team, working with units of the People's Defence Force, claimed the attack. The junta did not name who launched the drones in the statements cited.

title: Three US service members killed in one-way drone attack on Tower 22 outpost in northeast Jordan
place: Tower 22 logistics outpost, northeast Jordan near the Syrian border
summary: On 28 January 2024 a one-way attack drone struck a US logistics outpost known as Tower 22 in northeast Jordan, near the Syrian border. US Central Command said three US service members were killed and at least 34 were injured. It was the first attack on US forces in Jordan since the Israel-Hamas war began and the first in the region to kill US troops since then.
impact: CENTCOM said three US service members were killed and at least 34 injured, with eight evacuated from Jordan in stable condition; about 350 US Army and Air Force personnel were deployed at the base. Jordan's government said none of its own troops were hurt.
evidence: CENTCOM described a one-way attack UAS that impacted the base, and Jordan's government spokesperson said the attack was carried out by a drone. Reporting says it is unclear why air defences did not intercept the drone. The outpost is not publicly disclosed by Jordan.
unknown: Which group launched the drone and from where, and why it was not intercepted. The injury figure was expected to fluctuate as personnel received follow-on care.
attribution: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, a network of Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, claimed credit for the attack, according to Task & Purpose; The War Zone reports the group said it attacked other US bases in Syria and an Israeli naval facility, without naming Tower 22 in the statement it quotes. The US president said the attack was carried out by radical Iran-backed militant groups operating in Syria and Iraq and did not name a specific group.
